newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-Branson leads fight against BA/AMR link-up.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Branson leads fight against BA/AMR link-up.

text.p: Virgin Airlines chairman Richard Branson said on Monday the European Commission should block an alliance between British Airways and AMR Corp's American Airlines as a threat to transatlantic competition.
Branson indicated that he would be leading a charge against the planned deal at a Commission hearing on Tuesday called to garner interested parties' views on the alliance.
"We are urging the Commission to stop it," Branson told Reuters in Brussels where he was preparing for the Tuesday hearing.
"The only way you could redresss the balance is, at least, to have another carrier with the same number of slots and (flight) frequencies," he said.

The closed-door hearing started on Monday with BA and American defending the alliance. It followed weeks of angry exchanges between the Commission and the British authorities over who has the legal competence to examine the proposed transatlantic deal.
Others attending the hearing include representatives from Delta Air Lines, United Airlines, USAir and Continental Airlines.
European airlines, most of which are still state controlled, were being represented mainly by their governments.

Branson said BA and American would control nearly 80 percent of the routes between Britain and the United States. Virgin would come second with 10 percent of the traffic followed by United Airlines with a nine percent share.

The Commission is not expected to reach a final conclusion on the agreement before March. But expectations are that the British Department of Trade and Industry could clear the deal altogether in the coming weeks, setting the stage for a legal battle with the EU's competition watchdog.

The UK's Office of Fair Trading, which drafts the decision for the British government, proposed in December clearing the alliance provided the two airlines agreed to give up 168 weekly landing and taking off slots at the busy London Heathrow airport.

This has met harsh criticism from the Commission which made it clear that the proposal as it stood did not fully address all competiton concerns. It also clearly stated that under EU civil aviation rules slots could only be surrendered, not sold, as seems to be BA's intention.
U.S. competitors have also strongly argued that 168 slots would hardly compensate for the elimination of competition on the U.S.-British route.

European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert has warned that unless the Commission and Britain come to a similar assessment of the deal, the issue will most likely end up in the European Court of Justice. -- Brussels Newsroom 32 2 287 6800
